intro.carita: Madhyama Carita (the middle episode, chapters 2–4). In the recitation tradition its presiding form is Mahālakṣmī: the Gita Press viniyoga recited before 2.1 names Viṣṇu its ṛṣi, Mahālakṣmī its deity, uṣṇik its metre, Śākambharī its śakti and Durgā its bīja, and the dhyāna pictures Mahālakṣmī, seated on a lotus, holding eighteen objects as the crusher of the buffalo (सैरिभमर्दिनी). This is liturgical tradition, not a statement of the Purāṇa text, which never uses the name Mahālakṣmī in this chapter.
intro.summary: Medhas begins the second story (2.1). For a hundred years the gods under Indra fought the asuras under Mahiṣa; the gods were routed and Mahiṣāsura made himself Indra (2.2–3). The defeated gods, with Brahmā at their head, went to Śiva and Viṣṇu and told them everything: Mahiṣa holds the offices of the Sun, Indra, Fire, Wind, Moon, Yama and Varuṇa, and the gods, cast out of heaven, wander the earth like mortals; they take refuge and ask that his death be planned (2.4–8). Viṣṇu and Śiva grew angry, and a great radiance (tejas) came from the faces of Viṣṇu, Brahmā and Śiva and from the bodies of the other gods; it merged into one, blazed like a mountain on fire, and became a woman whose light filled the three worlds (2.9–13). Each god’s radiance formed a part of her body, and the auspicious one, Śivā, arose (2.14–18); the gods rejoiced (2.19). They armed her with weapons drawn from their own — Śiva’s trident, Viṣṇu’s discus, Varuṇa’s conch and noose, Agni’s spear, the Wind’s bow and quivers, Indra’s thunderbolt and Airāvata’s bell, Yama’s staff, a rosary and a water-pot, Time’s sword and shield — and adorned her with jewels, garments and garlands; Himavat gave her a lion, Kubera a cup never empty of wine, Śeṣa a serpent-necklace (2.20–31). She roared again and again with laughter; the sky, the worlds, the seas, the earth and the mountains shook; the gods cried ‘Victory!’ to the lion-rider and the sages praised her (2.32–35). The asuras rose in arms; Mahiṣāsura rushed towards the sound and saw her filling the three worlds, her crown touching the sky, her thousand arms spread through the directions (2.35–39). The battle began, and the text calls the roll of Mahiṣa’s generals — Cikṣura, Cāmara, Udagra, Mahāhanu, Asiloman, Bāṣkala, Biḍāla and others — with forces counted in ayutas and crores, and Mahiṣāsura himself in their midst (2.39–47). Their weapons she cut down as if in play, unwearied, and loosed her own (2.48–51); her lion raged through their ranks like fire through a forest, and her breaths became hosts (gaṇas) by the hundred thousand, who fought and beat the drums of a ‘festival of war’ (2.51–55). With trident, mace, sword, bell and noose she struck the great asuras down; headless trunks fought on and danced and cried ‘Stand!’ (2.55–64). The field became impassable and ran with rivers of blood (2.65–66); in a moment Ambikā consumed the army as fire consumes straw and timber (2.67); the lion roared among the fallen (2.68), and the gods in heaven rained down flowers (2.69). Mahiṣāsura himself is left for chapter 3.
intro.forms: The radiance of all the gods become a woman, filling the three worlds with her light (नारी, 2.13); Śivā, ‘the auspicious’, the name given her as her body is completed (2.18); the armed and adorned Devī who receives every god’s weapon (2.20–31); the lion-rider, सिंहवाहिनी, hailed with ‘Victory!’ (2.34); the cosmic form Mahiṣa sees, the earth bowed beneath her tread and her crown grazing the sky, a thousand arms in every direction (2.37–39); Caṇḍikā, ‘the fierce’ (2.49); Īśvarī, ‘the sovereign’, as she turns to the attack (2.51); and Ambikā, ‘the Mother’, the warrior whose breath becomes an army and who consumes the asura host (2.52, 2.67).
intro.significance: The first carita showed the Goddess as Mahāmāyā within Viṣṇu; this chapter shows her taking a body and weapons. The gods, separately, have lost everything; their anger and their pooled radiance become one being, and the gifts they give her are drawn out of their own weapons. Medhas has already said that she is eternal and is called ‘born’ only when she appears for the gods’ purpose (1.64–66), so the chapter is read as her manifestation, not her creation; the gods’ own hymn in chapter 4 calls her form the gathered power of all the hosts of gods (4.3). The chapter destroys Mahiṣa’s armies and leaves the buffalo-asura himself for chapter 3.
intro.grammar: Narrative perfects in great number, with every kind of reduplication (ददौ, ददृशुः, चुक्षुभुः, तुष्टुवुः, निजघान) and the unreduplicated e-perfects (चेलुः, पेतुः, वेमुः); periphrastic perfects of derived stems (कथयामासुः, 2.5; पातयामास, 2.56); past participles in place of finite verbs (पराजितम्, गताः, सम्भूताः) and the past active participle दत्तवान् alternating with ददौ in the list of gifts; the instrumental of source in the forming of her body (विष्णुतेजसा, सौम्येन, 2.14–17); a locative absolute at the opening (महिषे … अधिपे, 2.2) and in the battle (छिन्ने … शिरसि, 2.62); a passive imperative as a polite request (विचिन्त्यताम्, 2.8); long catalogues that run across verse boundaries, some with no verb of their own (2.16, 2.24–29, 2.40–48); numbers in ayutas, niyutas and crores; and epic (ārṣa) forms — parasmaipada युयुधुः and भाषन्तः from ātmanepada roots, अददत्, विचिन्वति, the genitive of the recipient (तस्याः, 2.24).
intro.teaching: Literally, defeated gods appeal to the great gods, a woman is formed from their combined radiance and armed with their weapons, and she destroys an asura army with her lion and her hosts. As teaching, the tradition reads the chapter as showing that the divine powers which fail when they act apart are, gathered together, one power — and that this power is hers, not theirs: she is eternal and only takes visible form for the gods’ purpose (1.64–66), the weapons they give are drawn out of their own, and the army that fights for her is her own breath (2.52–53), as she herself says later that there is no one but her (10.5). Her action is play (लीलयैव, 2.50), without strain. The gods’ part is to take refuge (2.8) and to praise; the asuras’ part is to meet her as a disturbance to be put down (2.36).
themes: Refuge: the defeated gods turn for help
Tejas: the gods’ powers made one in the Goddess
The arming of the Devī with the gods’ own weapons
Līlā: the battle as effortless play
Her hosts are her own power

conclusion.narrative: The gods have lost heaven to Mahiṣāsura and wander the earth. Their report rouses Viṣṇu and Śiva to anger, and from that anger and from every god the radiance pours out that becomes a woman, the auspicious Śivā. The gods arm and adorn her from their own weapons and treasures; her roar shakes the worlds, and Mahiṣa, rushing to the sound, sees her as wide as the cosmos. His generals and their uncountable armies attack; she cuts down their weapons as if in play, her breath becomes an army, and in a moment the whole host is consumed. The chapter ends with flowers falling from heaven and Mahiṣāsura himself still to be faced (2.69).

vocabulary.en: radiance, fiery power: what each god gives to form the Goddess
refuge; शरणं प्रपद् ‘to go for refuge’
office, function: the posts of the gods that Mahiṣa seizes
woman: what the gathered radiance became
the auspicious one: the Goddess named as her body is completed
she whose mount is the lion

play, ease: लीलयैव ‘as if in play’

constructions: The perfect as the narrative past, with its reduplications (ददौ, चुक्षुभुः, तुष्टुवुः, निजघान) and the unreduplicated e-perfects (चेलुः, पेतुः, वेमुः).
The periphrastic perfect of derived stems: कथयामासुः (2.5), पातयामास (2.56).
Participles for finite verbs: पराजितम्, गताः, सम्भूताः; and दत्तवान् ‘he gave’ beside ददौ in the gift list (2.20–31).
The instrumental of source: याम्येन … केशाः, विष्णुतेजसा बाहवः (2.14), changing to a predicate nominative in 2.18 (भ्रुवौ … संध्ययोः तेजः).
The locative absolute: महिषे असुराणाम् अधिपे (2.2), छिन्ने शिरसि (2.62).
The passive imperative as a request to superiors: वधः तस्य विचिन्त्यताम् (2.8).
Absolutives in -त्वा without a prefix (जित्वा, दृष्ट्वा, बद्ध्वा) and in -य with one (पुरस्कृत्य, निशम्य, समुत्पाद्य, आभाष्य).
Epic (ārṣa) forms beside the classical: parasmaipada युयुधुः (2.46, 2.48) and भाषन्तः (2.64), अददत् (2.29), विचिन्वति (2.68), the genitive of the recipient (तस्याः, 2.24).
insights: The Goddess appears from the radiance of all the gods made one (2.10–13), yet the text has already said she is eternal and only manifests for the gods’ purpose (1.64–66): their powers give her a visible form; they do not bring her into being.
Her weapons are drawn out of the gods’ own weapons (2.20, 2.22, 2.23), as her body was drawn out of their light (2.14–18): she bears every god’s power at once.
Her helpers are her own power: her breaths become the hosts who fight for her, made mighty by the Devī’s śakti (2.52–54).
Her action is play: she cuts down the whole armoury ‘as if in play’, her face unwearied (2.50), and consumes a vast army in a moment (2.67).
One manifestation, two responses: the sages bow and praise, the asuras see the worlds in turmoil and arm themselves (2.35–36).
conclusion.srividya: There are real, specific parallels with the Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa), noted on the verses: the emergence of the Goddess for the gods’ purpose (4, चिदग्निकुण्डसम्भूता; 5, देवकार्यसमुद्यता; with 2.13 — there from a fire-pit, here from the gods’ tejas); the name Śivā (53, शिवा; 998, श्रीशिवा; with 2.18); the bearer of all weapons (530, सर्वायुधधरा; with 2.20–31); the Goddess raining weapons in battle (79, भण्डासुरेन्द्रनिर्मुक्तशस्त्रप्रत्यस्त्रवर्षिणी; with निजशस्त्रास्त्रवर्षिणी, 2.50); her army of śaktis (65, भण्डासुरवधोद्युक्तशक्तिसेनासमन्विता; with the gaṇas of 2.53–54); and the names Ambikā (295) and Caṇḍikā (755). The Lalitā Sahasranāma also has the name महालक्ष्मीः (210), the presiding form of this carita in the Gita Press liturgy, though the chapter’s text never uses it. The battles are different stories (Bhaṇḍāsura there, Mahiṣa’s armies here), and these are shared Śākta images and names, not evidence that one text depends on the other; no specifically Śrīvidyā doctrine is stated in this chapter.

key_verses.why: The gods end their complaint: they have come for refuge and ask that Mahiṣa’s death be thought out.
The matchless radiance born from all the gods’ bodies gathers in one place and becomes a woman, filling the three worlds with its light.
The forming of her body is completed, and the auspicious one, Śivā, arises from the radiance of all the gods.
She stands with a thousand arms spread through every quarter, and the battle with the enemies of the gods begins.
Raining her own weapons, she cuts theirs down as if in play, her face unwearied, praised by gods and seers.
Her breaths become hosts by the hundred thousand and fight with axes, bhindipālas, swords and paṭṭiśas.
In a moment Ambikā consumes the great asura army, as fire consumes a heap of straw and timber.

sandhi_patterns: Visarga sandhi is by far the commonest: -aḥ → -o before voiced sounds, -aḥ/-āḥ losing the visarga before vowels and voiced consonants, visarga → ś/s before c/t (तस्यास्तु, शम्भुश्च), r-visarga (पुनरुत्थिताः, 2.62), and the special rule for सः (स स्वयम्, 2.6; स ददर्श, 2.37).
Savarṇa-dīrgha across words and inside compounds (तत्रासुरैः, देवासुरम्); guṇa, vṛddhi and yaṇ less often; ayādi in ददावशून्यम् (2.30) and, with y dropped, त एव (2.53); āv in श्रवणावनिलस्य (2.18).

Consonant junctions: voicing of finals, t + ś → cch (यदभूच्छाम्भवम्, 2.14), t + c/j → palatal (केचिच्च, अददज्जलधिः), t + n/m → n (केचिन्निपतिताः, तन्महासैन्यम्), n + c → ṃś (यांश्च, मृदङ्गांश्च), doubling of n (तस्मिन्नयुध्यत, 2.44), and tuk before ch inside words (प्रचिच्छेद, विच्छिन्न).
Final m before a vowel is written joined but unchanged (हारमजरे, तामूचुः, त्रैलोक्यममरारयः). No sandhi exceptions are declared in this chapter.
samasa: Ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣas are the commonest (देवसैन्यम्, महिषासुरचेष्टितम्, घण्टास्वन), often nested inside larger compounds.

Bahuvrīhis of description, many with a feminine last member shortened before a masculine (धुतसटः, छिन्नग्रीवाः, विच्छिन्नजङ्घाः) and many containing a tatpuruṣa (व्याप्तलोकत्रयम्, किरीटोल्लिखिताम्बराम्, क्षोभिताशेषपातालाम्).
Karmadhārayas, including a rūpaka (युद्धमहोत्सवे, the battle as a festival, 2.55).
Itaretara dvandvas in the lists of weapons, limbs and forces (शस्त्रास्त्र, जङ्घोरू, रथनागहयैः).

Upapada tatpuruṣas with agent nouns and root-nouns (पिनाकधृक्, सिंहवाहिनी, निजशस्त्रास्त्रवर्षिणी, सुरद्विषाम्, पुष्पवृष्टिमुचः); tṛtīyā and nañ tatpuruṣas (घण्टास्वनविमोहितान्, अनायस्त); one avyayībhāva.
grammar_notes: The hypermetric pāda of 2.2 (महिषेऽसुराणामधिपे, nine syllables) is kept as every witness has it.
In 2.13 the participles and adjectives stay neuter, agreeing with तेजः, until the predicate नारी: it is the radiance that became a woman.
The gift list and the muster-roll run across verse boundaries (2.24–32, 2.40–49); several verses have no verb of their own (2.16, 2.24a, 2.25–26), and the anvaya supplies it.
Epic (ārṣa) forms are kept and explained, not corrected: युयुधुः (2.46, 2.48), भाषन्तः (2.64), अददत् (2.29), विचिन्वति (2.68), the genitive of the recipient (2.24).
परिवारितः is read as a general’s name in 2.43 but as the participle ‘surrounded’ in 2.45; the numbers अयुत, नियुत and कोटि are explained where they occur (2.41–46).
themes: Tejas made one: the manifestation of the Goddess
uncertain: 2.69: महासुरैः (Gita Press, kept) / तथासुरैः (GRETIL, Freund) — Textual Verification Required.
Interpretive doubts (not about the reading) are flagged on 2.10, 2.17, 2.20, 2.23, 2.24, 2.25, 2.33, 2.42, 2.43, 2.44, 2.48, 2.60 and 2.68.
2.45 carries the recension note: GRETIL’s Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa has additional verses there (and in 2.20 and 2.65) that the Gita Press 700 does not; nothing was added.
